Although retrieval can improve grounding, it also introduces privacy risks when the underlying knowledge base contains sensitive information. A RAG system may retrieve documents containing personally identifiable information and subsequently reproduce that information in generated responses. This study evaluates sensitive-information leakage and redaction-based privacy protection in a controlled biomedical RAG environment.\n<div>\n A privacy benchmark was constructed using the 1,000-example labeled subset of PubMedQA by augmenting a fixed subset of 178 documents with synthetic patient records containing fictitious names, phone numbers, email addresses, Social Security number-like identifiers, and medical record numbers. No real patient information was used. A total of 890 targeted extraction attacks were generated to evaluate whether a RAG pipeline could disclose these synthetic identifiers. The baseline system used Sentence-BERT embeddings, FAISS dense retrieval, and FLAN T5-base for answer generation.\n<\/div>\n<div>\n Under the initial controlled privacy benchmark, the standard RAG configuration disclosed the exact synthetic secret in 60.11% of extraction attacks. The target document was retrieved at rank 1 in 98.20% of attacks, and leakage among attacks with correct rank-1 retrieval was 61.21%. Deterministic redaction designed for the known synthetic identifier formats reduced exact-secret leakage to 0.00% while preserving retrieval and question-answering utility on the 178 modified documents.\n<\/div>\n<div>\n A second robustness experiment evaluated 250 balanced extraction attacks after sensitive identifiers were transformed into alternative formatting variants not recognized by the original format-specific redactor. Under this format shift, standard RAG and the original format-specific redaction both produced a 63.20% exact-secret leakage rate. In contrast, a broader rule-based privacy-aware redaction mechanism reduced measured exact-secret leakage to 0.00%. Retrieval performance remained effectively unchanged: Recall@5 was 99.44% and MRR was 99.16% for both basic and privacy-aware redaction in the final utility evaluation. Answer accuracy changed from 41.57% to 42.70%.&nbsp;\n<\/div>\n<div>\n These results demonstrate, within the controlled synthetic benchmark, that format-specific redaction can be brittle under representation changes even when it performs perfectly on known formats. Broader privacy-aware redaction substantially reduced exact disclosure without measurable retrieval degradation in the evaluated setting. The findings provide an empirical framework for studying privacy\u2013utility tradeoffs in retrieval-augmented biomedical question answering. Semantically equivalent facts expressed in narrative text, tables, page images, or Extensible Business Reporting Language (XBRL) should support consistent answers, whereas a disclosure may support a query only after becoming public. We formalise this combination as crossmodal evidence symmetry under a causal temporal boundary and introduce TempFinRAG, a multimodal temporal retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) framework for point-in-time financial question answering. Given a question, company, and as-of date, the framework enforces the information boundary defined by U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) filing availability; aligns page layout, text, table structure, and XBRL facts; retrieves time-valid evidence; executes auditable financial calculations; and generates a cited answer. A verifier checks temporal validity, claim support, numerical consistency, and the need to abstain. We further introduce TempFinQA, a point-in-time evaluation protocol built from public filings and XBRL facts, and evaluate the framework on complementary evidence-grounded, numerical, conversational, and multi-table benchmarks. On TempFinQA, TempFinRAG improves answer accuracy from 66.7% to 78.9% over hybrid RAG while reducing temporal evidence leakage from 10.8% to 1.7% and hallucination from 17.3% to 7.9%. Reliable financial question answering therefore requires consistent treatment across evidence representations and deliberately asymmetric access across
